pool.q: In addition to greater durability and easier maintenance, what is an advantage of rigid gas permeable lenses over soft contact lenses?
pool.rationale:
Unlike soft contact lenses, which conform to the shape of the cornea, rigid gas permeable (RGP) lenses are able to correct for irregular astigmatism because the rigid shape of the lens allows a tear lens to form behind it and "fill in" the corneal irregularities to improve the refractive surface.
RGP lenses are more expensive but tend to be more durable with simpler care than soft contact lenses. RGP lenses require a longer period of adaptation, are more uncomfortable, and are more difficult to fit than commercial soft contact lenses.

pool.q: What laser-tissue interaction is the basis of the effect of the excimer laser used in laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)?
pool.rationale:
Laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) and photorefractive keratectomy (PRK), common refractive surgeries of the cornea, are based on photoablation using excimer lasers that generate photons with wavelengths in the ultraviolet (UV) range that are absorbed within the corneal tissue.
Photocoagulation, which is associated with protein and collagen denaturation, is the most commonly used thermal laser–tissue interaction in ophthalmic surgery. The most common ophthalmic applications of photocoagulation include laser coagulation to prevent retinal detachments, photocoagulation of retinal vessel disease and panretinal photocoagulation in diabetic retinopathy.
The most important ophthalmic application of a photodisruptive interaction is posterior capsulotomy using the Nd:YAG laser. During a photodisruption procedure, it is the mechanical (acoustic) wave and not the laser light itself (as with plasma-induced ablation) that breaks the capsule.
Photochemical interaction, sometimes referred to as photoactivation, takes place at long exposure times, ranging from seconds to continuously, and very low power densities or irradiances (typically 1 W/cm2). This type of interaction is based on the use of a photo-sensitizing dye (eg, rose bengal, riboflavin, or verteporfin) that serves as a chemical (electron reaction) catalyst. Laser irradiation, at a wavelength coupled to the specific dye used, causes a photochemical reaction only within tissues where the dye is present and when irradiated.
Plasma-induced ablation is the principle upon which femtosecond lasers are based.

pool.q: A 3 PD base-in and a 4 PD base-up prism can be combined into a single prism. What would be the power of the combined prism?
pool.rationale: When combining multiple prisms, the vector and axis are calculated by using right-angle trigonometry (the Pythagorean theorem (a^2+b^2=c^2)). In this case, one vector would be 3 in the "x-axis" and one vector would be 4 in the "y-axis." This would create a right triangle with a resultant vector that is 5 (PD). The axis is calculated by the formula (theta = cos^-1 (a/c), where a = adjacent side, c=hypotenuse). The opposite and adjacent sides of the triangle are 4 and 3. Therefore, the hypotenuse is 5 (4^2+3^2 = 25 = c^2, c = 5). Then, the axis is the cos^-1(3/5) = 53 degrees.

pool.q: What are the characteristics of the intermediate image: upright or inverted, real or virtual, and transverse magnification?
pool.rationale:
The terms anterior focal point and posterior focal point can be confusing because, for minus lenses, the anterior focal point is actually behind the posterior focal point. The anterior focal point, Fa, is always in object space, and the posterior focal point, Fp, is always in image space. By convention, primed letters indicate image space and unprimed letters, object space. Often, the anterior focal point is designated F and the posterior focal point, F′. For a –1.00 D thin lens in air, F is 1.0 m behind the lens, and F′ is 1.0 m in front of the lens. For all thin lenses, the principal planes coincide. Likewise, the nodal points coincide.
The image features can be determined graphically, as shown in the figure. A ray from the tip of the object directed to F exits the lens parallel to the optical axis. A ray from the tip of the object parallel to the axis exits the lens divergent, as if it had come from F′. A ray from the tip of the object directed to the nodal points exits undeviated, and in this case, undisplaced, as shown in black below. The image characteristics—upright, virtual, and reduced—are apparent from this graphical approach.

pool.q: While performing streak retinoscopy, the examiner notes that the light reflex has an asymmetric "scissor" shape. What is the most likely explanation?

This is also a description of irregular astigmatism, which is often seen in patients with keratoconus. High myopia, hyperopia, and regular astigmatism will alter the "with" and "against" behavior of the reflex, but are not responsible for the scissors reflex.

pool.q: Following cataract surgery in the left eye, a patient has a refraction of right, −3.50 D; left, −0.50 D. The ophthalmologist prescribes spectacles with a +2.50 flat-top bifocal set 3 mm below the optical center of the lens. How much prism would need to be corrected when the patient is looking 4 mm below the top of the bifocal?

pool.q: LogMAR notation (base-10 logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution) is frequently used to record visual acuity in clinical trials. pool.q: A hyperopic patient is undergoing cataract surgery. Based on accurate biometry, a +31.0 D intraocular lens is selected to target a refractive spherical equivalent of plano. What is the approximate range of intraocular lens (IOL) power error possible, based on American National Standards Institute (ANSI) and International Standards Organization (ISO) standards?

pool.q: In a phakic eye, at what range of wavelengths is the retina susceptible to photochemical injury?
pool.rationale:
The cornea, lens, and retina are susceptible to injury at various wavelengths of light.
The cornea is susceptible to almost all wavelengths of light: UV light (180-400 nm) can cause photokeratitis, and visible and infrared light (400 nm-1 mm) can cause thermal injury.
The lens is susceptible to injury from UV light (180-400 nm), causing cataracts, as well as to thermal injury from light wavelengths 400-3000 nm.
The retina is susceptible to thermal injury from 400-1400 nm, and photochemical injury from blue light (400-550 nm, 310-550 nm for an aphakic eye). The susceptibility to damage from blue light is the basis for incorporating UV-blocking and blue-blocking chromophores in some intraocular lenses (IOLs).

pool.q: What adjustment should be made to the IOL power selection in an eye containing silicone oil?

options.a: Increase IOL power by 3-5 D if the silicone oil will be removed from the eye.
options.b: Decrease IOL power by 3-5 D if the silicone oil will remain in the eye.
options.c: Increase IOL power by 3-5 D if the silicone oil will remain in the eye.
options.d: Decrease IOL power by 3-5 D if the silicone oil will be removed from the eye.

pool.rationale:
Silicone oil can make IOL selection difficult for 2 reasons: obtaining measurements and selecting lenses. IOL measurements with an ultrasonic biometer can be unreliable, given the different ultrasound velocity for silicone oil (980 m/s) and vitreous (1532 m/s). Optical methods such as the IOLMaster are much more reliable.
If the silicone oil is to be removed from the eye in the near future, one can proceed with lens selection as usual. However, if the silicone oil is to remain in the eye, adjustments must be made. Silicone oil creates a negative lens power in the eye when coupled with a biconvex IOL, which is standard in the US. Most surgeons elect to increase IOL power by 3-5 diopters in order to avoid a hyperopic surprise. Of note, silicone lenses should not be used with silicone oil in the eye.

pool.q: A Galilean telescope is made with a –12.00 D eyepiece and a +6.00 D objective. What is the angular magnification of the telescope?
pool.rationale:
Angular magnification (MA) of a telescope is equal to the power of the eyepiece (FE) divided by the power of the objective (FO). MA = (-) FE / FO = (-) -12 / +6 = 2×  Galilean telescopes have a weak (+) objective lens with a strong (-) eyepiece lens. The lenses are separated by the difference of their focal lengths. An upright image is formed.
Galilean telescopes are usually 2× magnification. Surgical loupes and low vision aides are examples of Galilean telescopes. They are useful for low vision work because the image is upright, the device is short, inexpensive, weighs less, and has a large exit pupil, making centering easy.
The Keplerian telescope has a weak (+) objective lens and a strong (+) eyepiece lens. The lenses are separated by the sum of their focal lengths. An inverted image is formed so they need an erecting lens or prism. Keplerian telescopes are usually 4× magnification or stronger. An example of a Keplerian telescope is the astronomical telescope.

pool.q: What combination of optical elements is required to construct a Keplerian telescope that produces an upright image?

options.a: a lower-power (+) lens and a higher-power (+) lens, separated by the sum of their focal lengths
options.b: a lower-power (+) lens and a higher-power (+) lens, separated by the sum of their focal lengths, with an inverting prism
options.c: a lower-power (+) lens and a higher-power (-) lens, separated by the difference in their focal lengths, with an inverting prism
options.d: a lower-power (+) lens and a higher-power (-) lens, separated by the difference in their focal lengths

pool.rationale:
A lower-power (+) lens and a higher-power (+) lens, separated by the sum of their focal lengths, produces a Keplerian telescope. A Keplerian telescope produces an inverted image; therefore, inverting prisms are required to make an upright image. Most binoculars are made from Keplerian telescopes with inverting prisms.
A lower-power (+) lens and a higher-power (-) lens, separated by the difference in their focal lengths, produces a Galilean telescope. A Galilean telescope produces an upright image; therefore, no inverting prism is required.

pool.q: A red light and a green light are each projected through a 1 mm aperture. What best describes the effects of diffraction with each light?

options.a: The green light will converge more than the red light.
options.b: The red light will converge more than the green light.
options.c: The green light will diverge more than the red light.
options.d: The red light will diverge more than the green light.

pool.rationale: Diffraction describes the divergence of light as it traverses through an aperture. The smaller the aperture is relative to the wavelength of light, the more pronounced the diffraction. As such, red light (longer wavelength) will experience more diffraction than green light (shorter wavelength). Although it is true that in refraction, green light (shorter wavelength light) will converge in front of red light (longer wavelength light); this is due to chromatic aberration of the eye, rather than diffraction.

pool.q: While surfing, a person spots a shark nearby in the water. Where is the shark, in reality, compared with where the person sees its image from the surfboard?

options.c: the same distance, but to the opposite side

pool.rationale:
If light travels from a denser medium (in this case, water) to a less dense medium (in this case, air), then light rays bend away from the surface normal (according to Snell's law). This redirection of light produces image displacement, thus causing the shark to appear further away than it actually is (therefore, it actually is closer than it appears).
However, for a shark (in the water) looking up at a surfer (in the air), the surfer would actually be further from the shark than the surfer appeared.

pool.q: Why are daily-wear contact lenses favored over extended-wear lenses in the United States?

options.a: better quality of vision with daily-wear lenses
options.b: longer period of adaptation with extended-wear lenses
options.c: increased risk of keratitis with extended-wear lenses
options.d: better correction of astigmatism with daily-wear lenses

pool.rationale:
Daily-wear lenses have been favored in the US ever since reports in the 1980s showed increased incidence of keratitis with extended-wear lenses.
Additional risk factors for extended wear complications include previous eye infections, lens use while swimming, exposure to smoke, dry eye, eyelid margin disease, and allergy. Daily-wear users are exposed to the same risks, only less so.
About 10% of contact lenses fitted in the US are rigid gas-permeable (RGP) lenses. The main advantages of RGP lenses are the high quality of vision they offer, including the correction of corneal astigmatism, as well as durability and simplicity of lens care. The main disadvantages of RBP contact lenses are initial discomfort, longer period of adaptation, greater knowledge and effort required for fitting, and the greater cost of replacing a lost or damaged lens.

pool.q: A patient with macular degeneration reports blurred vision at near. His visual acuity is 20/160 in each eye with no refractive error in either eye. What is the most appropriate prescription for low-vision reading glasses?

options.a: OD: +4.00 sphere 8 BI OS: +4.00 sphere 8 BI
options.b: OD: +8.00 sphere 10 BI OS: +8.00 sphere 10 BI
options.c: OD: +4.00 sphere 4 BI OS: +4.00 sphere 4 BI
options.d: OD: +8.00 sphere 8 BI OS: +8.00 sphere 8 BI

pool.rationale:
OS: +8.00 sphere 10 BI

In patients with low visual acuity, high-plus reading glasses may be helpful reading aids. The Kestenbaum rule provides the dioptric power of the reading lens, which is defined by the following equation:

[Lens dioptric power] = 1 / [visual acuity fraction]

In this case, the lens dioptric power would be 160/20, which is +8.00 diopters.

Because of the high power of the lens, prisms are added to help reduce convergence. As a general rule, the amount of prism added to the glasses is 2 prism diopters base-in more than the dioptric power of the lens, or in this case, 10 base-in in each eye.

pool.q: What is the effect of common refractive errors on the apparent size of the optic disc as seen with a direct ophthalmoscope?

options.a: The optic disc will appear smaller in a myopic eye than a hyperopic eye.
options.b: The optic disc will appear smaller in a myopic eye than an emmetropic eye.
options.c: The optic disc will appear larger in a hyperopic eye than an emmetropic eye.
options.d: The optic disc will appear smaller in an aphakic eye than an emmetropic eye.

pool.rationale: With direct ophthalmoscopy, the examiner uses the optics of the patient’s eye as a simple magnifier to look at the retina. The optics of the normal eye are approximately +60 D, so using the formula for a simple magnifier, the magnification is 60/4, or 15×. If the patient’s eye is myopic, a minus lens is dialed in, to overcome the extra plus power “error lens” inside the patient’s eye. Those 2 lenses create a Galilean telescope effect, increasing magnification and decreasing the field of view. Similarly, the retina of a hyperopic eye will be magnified less than 15× because of the reverse Galilean telescope created by the minus power error lens inside the patient’s eye and the plus lens of the direct ophthalmoscope. Thus, the size of the optic disc will appear smaller in a hyperopic eye—of which aphakia is an extreme example—than in an emmetropic eye or a myopic eye.

pool.q: A cycloplegic streak retinoscopy is performed on a nonverbal, adult patient at a testing distance of 67 cm. The result for the right eye is as follows:+3 D sphere neutralizes the reflex when the streak is horizontal (180°); +4 D sphere neutralizes the reflex when the streak is vertical (90°). What refraction is correct for the right eye?
pool.rationale: If the retinoscopy streak is horizontal, the axis of the cylindrical lens is also horizontal (180°). So the spherocylindrical lens combination for this patient, before subtracting the working distance adjustment, is +3.00 +1.00 × 90. The working distance (67 cm, or 0.67 m) must be subtracted from the final refraction. Thus subtracting 1/0.67 m, or 1.50 D, yields the correct answer: +1.50 +1.00 × 90. Note that the cylindrical power acts 90° from the axis. If the retinoscopy streak is horizontal, the axis of the cylindrical lens is 180°, but the actual power is at 90°. Accordingly the powers, after subtracting the working distance, are +1.50 D at 90° and +2.50 D at 180°.

pool.q: In the schematic eye, certain simplifications are done to make the calculations less cumbersome. In the reduced schematic eye, the retinal image size is calculated from the actual height of a Snellen letter on the eye chart, the distance from the eye chart to the eye, and the distance from the nodal point to the retina using what geometric principle?

pool.q: What part of an intraocular lens (IOL) is typically responsible for a patient experiencing glare?
pool.rationale:
The presence of IOLs may cause numerous optical phenomena. Various light-related visual phenomena encountered by pseudophakic patients are termed dysphotopsias. These phenomena are divided into positive and negative dysphotopsias. Positive dysphotopsias are characterized by brightness, streaks, and rays emanating from a central point source of light, sometimes with a diffuse, hazy glare. Such optical phenomena may be related to light reflection and refraction along the edges of the IOL. High-index acrylic lenses with square or truncated edges produce a more intense edge glare. These phenomena may also be due to internal re-reflection within the IOL itself; such reflection is more likely to occur with materials that have a higher refractive index, such as acrylic. With a less steeply curved anterior surface, the lens may be more likely to have internal reflections that are directed toward the fovea and are therefore more distracting.
Multifocal optics can cause image degradation, "ghost" images, decreased contrast sensitivity, and reduced performance in low light. They do not tend to produce glare.

pool.q: What is the typical age of stabilization of myopia in the US?
pool.rationale: In the US, the mean rate of childhood myopia progression is reported at about 0.50 D per year. In approximately 75% of teenagers, refractive errors stabilize at about age 15 to 16 years. In those whose errors do not stabilize, progression often continues into the 20s or 30s.

pool.q: An aphakic patient requests counseling on correction for his refractive error. What correction would result in the least image magnification?

With aphakic spectacles, image magnification can be as high as 20%–35%. Contact lenses can still magnify images by 7%–12%. An anterior chamber IOL can still cause up to 5% magnification. A posterior chamber IOL would have the least amount of magnification, because it is closer to the nodal point.

The new distance spectacle power is found to be –5.50 D in both eyes. He expresses an interest in contact lenses. What is the likely effect on both reading and distance vision of changing the distance correction?

options.b: He will find it difficult to read with single-vision spectacles, –5.50 OU, and even more difficult to read with contact lenses that correct his distance vision.

In this age range (eg, 46 years of age), people with myopia who are still able to read with their correct distance glasses are likely to find it more difficult to read with contact lenses. pool.q: What is the definition of n, the refractive index?

options.a: speed of light in water / speed of light in a vacuum
options.b: speed of light in a medium / speed of light in air
options.c: speed of light in a vacuum / speed of light in a medium
options.d: speed of light in air / speed of light in water

pool.rationale: The speed of light in a vacuum is one of the fundamental constants of nature. The speed of light in air is essentially the same. It is convenient to refer to the speed of light in other materials by comparison to the speed of light in a vacuum: the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in another medium is referred to as the refractive index of the medium. We abbreviate the refractive index as n.

pool.q: Past what point does a toric intraocular lens (IOL) have to be rotated before it increases the residual astigmatism of the eye rather than reduces it?
pool.rationale:
Intraocular lenses with a toric surface are used to correct astigmatism. However, they must be appropriately aligned with the axis they are supposed to correct in order to have the optimal effect. When toric lenses are implanted in the vertical axis, there are more rotational stability concerns than when they are implanted in the horizontal axis.
If the toric lens rotates away from the optimal desired angle, the benefit of the toric lens diminishes until it eventually increases the residual astigmatism of the eye. At angles greater than 30° off-axis, the residual astigmatism increases; if the lens is 90° off-axis, the residual astigmatism doubles.

pool.q: What does Dk/t describe in a contact lens?

options.a: oxygen storage capacity of the lens
options.b: oxygen absorption rate of the lens
options.d: oxygen permeability of the lens material

pool.rationale: Dk, Dk/t, and wetting angle are some terms used to describe oxygen permeability and wettability: Dk refers to the oxygen permeability of a lens material, where D is the diffusion coefficient for oxygen movement in the material, and k is the solubility constant of oxygen in the material. Dk/t refers to the oxygen transmissibility of a lens, depending on its material and central thickness (t). Wetting angle refers to the wettability of a lens surface. A low wetting angle means water will spread over the surface, increasing surface wettability. Both a high Dk/t and a low wetting angle are desirable.

pool.q: What axis is depicted in green?
pool.rationale: The green line refers to the visual axis, which is a line made between a fixation target and the fovea. The optical axis (blue) is defined as a line that passes through the center of the cornea and lens. The pupillary axis (red) is defined as a line that passes perpendicular to the cornea and through the center of the pupil. Angle kappa (not shown) is the angle between the pupillary and visual axis.

pool.q: What is the procedure for measuring the distance correction of spectacles in a lensmeter?

options.a: The back vertex of the lens is measured with the temple of the spectacles pointing toward the examiner.
options.b: The front vertex of the lens is measured with the temple of the spectacles pointing away from the examiner.
options.c: The front vertex of the lens is measured with the temple of the spectacles pointing toward the examiner.
options.d: The back vertex of the lens is measured with the temple of the spectacles pointing away from the examiner.

pool.rationale:
A lensmeter, or lensometer, uses a fixed lens to measure the power of an unknown lens. The observer looks through an astronomical telescope, which magnifies the target image and reduces the observer’s accommodation or refractive error.
The spectacles are placed with the rear vertex of the distance lens on the nose cone, with the temple of the spectacles facing away from the examiner; this is because the lensmeter is calibrated to read the rear vertex power of the distance spectacle lens. The target is moved until the target appears in focus, and the power of the lens is read on the dial. Of note, to read lined bifocal spectacles, the spectacles are turned around so the front vertex of the add lens is read, and the difference between the distance and near portions are used to determine the add power of the lens.

pool.q: The refraction of + 2.00 + 1.50 x 90 indicates what type of astigmatism?
pool.rationale:
Astigmatism is typically caused by a toric-shaped cornea. If there is regular astigmatism, 1 meridian of the cornea is the flattest and perpendicular (90 degrees away) from 1 meridian that is the steepest. One way of classifying astigmatism is by the location of the focal lines within the eye.
Simple astigmatism refers to 1 focal line on the retina and 1 line either in front of the retina (simple myopic astigmatism) or behind the retina (simple hyperopic astigmatism).
Compound astigmatism results if both focal lines are either in front of the retina (compound myopic astigmatism) or behind the retina (compound hyperopic astigmatism). In the scenario described, the + 2.00 + 1.50 x 90 refraction means both focal lines would focus behind the retina.
Mixed astigmatism results if the focal lines are on both sides of the retina (straddling the retina). Against-the-rule astigmatism is defined as astigmatism that can be corrected with a plus cylinder between 150 and 30 degrees.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Clinical Optics & Vision Rehabilitation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Following laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), a patient complains of glare and halos during night driving. Aside from pilocarpine, what topical medication may be useful in reducing these symptoms?
pool.rationale: Irregular astigmatism after refractive surgery can cause glare and halo and starbursts. Newer lasers have dramatically decreased the incidence and severity of night-vision problems; however, spherical aberration that is increased after laser vision correction can still cause problems with visual quality. Using a miotic such as brimonidine (0.2%) or pilocarpine (0.5%-1%) may be quite useful in these patients by reducing the pupil size, thereby mitigating the glare.

pool.q: Assuming a standard reference distance (25 cm), what power lens will provide a magnification of 2.5x?
pool.rationale:
The angular magnification ("power" or "magnification power") of a lens is calculated by the equation

[Lens dioptric power] / [dioptric equivalent of the reference distance]

In this scenario, the lens dioptric power can be solved:

L / 4 = 2.5 D

L = 10.0 D

pool.q: A patient would like to obtain his contact lens prescription from an internet-based service provider. What is the duty of the provider to verify the prescription under the Federal Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act (PL 108-14)?

options.a: The contact lens prescriber is required to verify the prescription with the seller with a phone call or fax within a week.
options.b: The contact lens prescription is considered automatically verified if the prescriber does not respond within 8 business hours Monday-Friday, except federal holidays.
options.c: The provider must update the refraction with a repeat in-office examination, and a paper copy can then be supplied.
options.d: Prescriptions created by one office may not be transferred to a third party and will need to be dispensed by the office.

If the patient calls in contact lens parameters to a seller, and the seller leaves a message for the prescriber, it is considered “verified” if the prescriber doesn’t reply within 8 business hours, Monday – Friday, except federal holidays. pool.q: What lens design would lead to a higher rate of capsular opacification?

options.a: lens with a square, truncated edge
options.c: lens with an annular, ridge edge

pool.rationale: Intraocular lenses (IOLs) with an annular, ridge edge or a square, truncated edge create a barrier effect at the optic edge that reduces posterior capsular opacification (PCO). Older lenses that had been used before the modern sharp edge design that also decreased PCO were partial-ridge and meniscus IOLs.

pool.q: What combination of intraocular lens (IOL) characteristics would be expected to minimize dysphotopsias?
pool.rationale: Various light-related visual phenomena may be experienced by pseudophakic patients. These optical phenomena are termed dysphotopsias. High-index IOLs (eg, acrylic) with square edges produce more intense edge glare and also cause optical phenomena secondary to internal re-reflection. Use of IOLs with lower refractive indices and smoother edges may decrease the occurrence of these dysphotopsias.

pool.q: A 29-year-old previously myopic woman presents to a clinic in one state for a second opinion after undergoing laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) 3 months prior in another state. She reports that after the surgery, her vision still is not sharp. Upon performing retinoscopy, the ophthalmologist sees a scissoring reflex. What refractive abnormality is suspected?
pool.rationale: A "scissoring" retinoscopy reflex indicates irregular astigmatism. Overcorrection of a myopic patient would result in hyperopia, which would demonstrate "with" motion on retinoscopy. Undercorrection would indicate that the patient still is myopic, which would demonstrate "against" motion on retinoscopy. Regular astigmatism (ie, astigmatism with a defined axis) results in oblique motion on retinoscopy if the streak is off axis, but scissoring of the reflex would not be expected.

pool.q: What is one method for transposing a prescription from minus to plus cylinder notation?

options.a: Subtract the cylinder from the sphere, switch the sign of the cylinder power, and rotate the axis 90 degrees.
options.b: Add the sphere and cylinder, switch the sign of the cylinder power, and rotate the axis 180 degrees.
options.c: Subtract the cylinder from the sphere, switch the sign of the cylinder power, and rotate the axis 180 degrees.
options.d: Add the sphere and cylinder, switch the sign of the cylinder power, and rotate the axis 90 degrees.

pool.rationale:
To transpose refractive errors within the 2 notations:
  1. Add the sphere and cylinder magnitude arithmetically: This is the new sphere power.
  2. Switch the cylinder sign; that is, make minus plus or make plus minus. The magnitude of the cylinder power remains the same.
  3. Change the axis of cylinder by 90 degrees.
The other answers are incorrect.

pool.q: What step can be taken to minimize image jump in the design of a bifocal?

options.a: placing the optical center of the segment as close as possible to the top of the segment
options.b: using a blended bifocal segment that has no visible line of separation
options.c: placing the top of the segment as close as possible to the distance optical center

pool.rationale: As the eyes look down to read through the add segment, there is an abrupt upward image jump at the top edge of the segment. This jump is due to the prismatic effect of the plus lens (the add segment). On the basis of the Prentice rule, the amount of jump depends on the power of the segment and on the distance from the top of the segment to the optical center of the segment.

pool.q: The normal human cornea has a shape that reduces spherical aberration of incoming rays. What is this shape and how does the curvature of the central cornea relate to the curvature of the peripheral cornea?

options.a: Prolate, steeper in the center than the periphery
options.b: Oblate, flatter in the center than the periphery
options.c: Prolate, flatter in the center than the periphery
options.d: Oblate, steeper in the center than the periphery

pool.rationale: The shape of the human cornea is prolate, meaning it is steeper in the center than the periphery. This asphericity reduces spherical aberration where peripheral rays have a nearer focal point than more central rays.

pool.q: A patient who has been prescribed new progressive add lenses returns with the complaint that he needs to tilt his chin up in order to see clearly at distance. What is the most likely source of the problem?

options.b: add power that is too strong
options.d: add power that is positioned too high

pool.rationale: In the chin-up position, the patient is effectively adding plus power to the distance prescription by viewing through the upper portion of the add. The patient has either undercorrected hyperopia or overcorrected myopia.

pool.q: What presbyopia-correcting lens may be more effective at higher lens powers?
pool.rationale: Accommodating IOLs such as the Crystalens link accommodative effort to an anterior shift in effective lens position. The higher the power of the IOL, the more effect an anterior movement (and change in effective lens position) will have. Refractive (ReZoom) and diffractive (ReSTOR and Symfony) IOLs have concentric rings that focus light at near and far points through refraction and diffraction, respectively. They largely rely on pupil diameter rather than effective lens position and are therefore less influenced by IOL power.

pool.q: What is the diameter of the pinhole aperture used in a pinhole occluder?
pool.rationale: The diameter of the pinhole aperture is 1.2 mm. The pinhole acts as a smaller pupil and reduces the size of the blur circle on the retina, sharpening the image. With diameters smaller than 1.2 mm, the blurring effects of diffraction overwhelm the sharpening effects of the smaller pupil.

pool.q: A patient has a refractive error of -4.50 D and a K measurement of 45.0 D (7.50 mm). What is the residual refractive error if a plano rigid contact lens with a base curve of 7.67 mm (44.0 D) is placed on the eye?
pool.rationale: The curvature of the contact lens (44.0 D) is flatter than the cornea (45.0 D) by 1 D. This means that the tear film creates a NEGATIVE lens power: -1.0 D. To counteract this tear film, +1.0 D must be added to the refraction: -4.50 D + 1.0 D = -3.50 D. This is popularly remembered by the SAM-FAP rule: Steeper Add Minus - Flatter Add Plus. Since the contact lens is flatter by 1.0 D, add +1.0 D to the refraction of -4.50 D for a power of -3.50 D.

pool.q: What lens parameters could be changed to decrease lens movement in a soft contact lens that moves excessively with eyelid blinking?

options.a: flattening the base curve while maintaining the diameter
options.b: steepening the base curve while maintaining the diameter
options.c: increasing the power of the contact lens
options.d: decreasing the diameter while maintaining the base curve

pool.rationale: Increasing the sagittal depth of the contact lens tightens the fit and decreases lens movement, which may be achieved through steepening (decreasing) the base curve or increasing the diameter of the contact lens. Flattening (increasing) the base curve or decreasing the diameter of the lens decreases sagittal depth and increases the movement of the lens on the cornea. The power of the contact lens should not affect the fitting relationships.

pool.q: What pediatric age group has the highest prevalence of myopia in the United States?
pool.rationale:
The refractive state of the eye changes during normal development. In general, eyes become more hyperopic until approximately 7 years of age, at which point they tend to become more myopic as the axial length increases and the lens and cornea flatten until they reach their final adult dimensions.
The BCSC cites the following rates of myopia in the United States:
  • 5-7 years old: 3%
  • 8-10 years old: 8%
  • 11-12 years old: 14%
  • 12-17 years old: 25%
Also note that different ethnic groups have different rates of myopia. Although only 25% of US adolescents aged 12 to 17 years have myopia, in Taiwan 84% of adolescents aged 16 to 18 years are myopic, with similar high prevalence rates among other Asian countries, such as Japan and Singapore. For individuals who develop adult-onset myopia, extensive near work is a major risk factor.

pool.q: What type of contact lens would most likely provide the best optical correction for a patient with 4 diopters of regular corneal astigmatism?

options.c: rigid gas permeable (RGP) spherical contact lens
options.d: rigid gas permeable (RGP) toric contact lens

pool.rationale: Patients with more than 3 D of corneal astigmatism should be fitted with a toric rigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lens. Spherical RGP lenses can be used to correct up to 3 D of corneal astigmatism. Most toric soft contact lenses can correct up to 2 D of corneal astigmatism, although custom soft toric lenses can be made to correct higher amounts. "Front toric" and "back toric" refer to the surface where the astigmatism correction is placed on the soft toric contact lens.

pool.q: What is the approximate speed of light in a vacuum?
pool.rationale: The exact speed of light in a vacuum is 299,792,458 m/s, which is often approximated to 300,000,000 (3 x 108) m/s.

pool.q: What is photometry?

options.a: the measurement of electromagnetic (EM) radiation between microwave and soft x-ray wavelengths
options.b: the measurement of the human visual system's psychophysical response to light
options.c: the measurement of photons emitted by the absorption of an energy stimulus
options.d: the measurement of light sensitivity against a uniform background

pool.rationale: Photometry is a type of radiometry that helps describe how the eye responds to different wavelengths of light. In essence, it measures the human visual system's psychophysical response to light. Radiometry in general measures EM radiation between microwave and soft x-ray wavelengths but does not provide any reference to how that radiation affects the human visual system. The measurement of light sensitivity against a uniform background describes perimetry, which is the process of measuring visual fields. The measurement of photons emitted by the absorption of an energy stimulus refers to fluorescence.

pool.q: A 4-year-old boy has best corrected visual acuity of 20/100 in the setting of albinism. In addition to prescribing the appropriate refractive correction, what intervention should be recommended?

options.c: lensectomy with implantation of the appropriate intraocular lens

pool.rationale: Children with visual impairment need to acquire many vision-aided life skills (eg, reading, understanding social cues, self care) that adults with visual impairment often already have developed. Therefore, visual rehabilitation always should be recommended for children with visual impairment. The other options listed would not be recommended treatments for this child, as (1) there is no concern for cataract, and lensectomy would not be expected to improve the vision, (2) if he has nystagmus, then it likely is a sensory nystagmus without associated oscillopsia, and thus does not need treatment, and (3) there currently is no gene therapy available for this condition.

pool.q: What is the appropriate spectacle lens prescription for a completely blind eye?

options.a: the same prescription as the seeing eye
options.b: minus lens to minify the appearance

pool.rationale: A "balance lens" may be specified for a completely blind eye. This allows the dispensing optician to place a lens that is cosmetically similar to the fellow eye. In some cases, this may lessen the cost of the lens for the patient. Care must be taken in prescribing this for an eye with limited but usable vision.

pool.q: What would be the best approach to choosing intraocular lens (IOL) power in a patient who required cataract surgery and penetrating keratoplasty?

options.a: Wait for the transplant to heal completely before implanting an IOL.
options.b: Use the K reading of the fellow eye.
options.c: Use a power commensurate with the eye's axial length and refractive error.
options.d: Use the average K value of a previous series of transplants.

pool.rationale:
It is very difficult to predict the ultimate power of the cornea after the eye has undergone PK. Thus, in 1987 Hoffer recommended that the surgeon wait for the corneal transplant to heal completely before implanting an IOL. The current safety of intraocular surgery allows for such a double-procedure approach in all but the rarest cases.
If simultaneous IOL implantation and corneal transplant are necessary, surgeons may use either the K reading of the fellow eye or the average postoperative K value of a previous series of transplants, but these approaches are fraught with error. When there is corneal scarring in an eye but no need for a corneal graft, it might be best to use the corneal power of the other eye or even a power that is commensurate with the eye's axial length and refractive error.

pool.q: Because of the refractive effects of the cornea, the image of the pupil when viewed by the clinician is not the same size as the actual pupil. The image seen by the clinician is called the entrance pupil. The entrance pupil varies from the actual pupil by what amount?
pool.rationale: Because the cornea has a high plus power, the image of the pupil is 13% to 15% larger than the actual pupil. The actual amount varies, depending on anterior chamber depth and corneal curvature.

pool.q: A 3-year-old child is found to have age-appropriate visual acuity and is +1.50 sphere hyperopic in each eye on cycloplegic refraction. She is orthotropic on alternate cover test. What is recommended next in her management?
pool.rationale: Unless there is an esodeviation or evidence of reduced vision, it is not necessary to correct low hyperopia in children. Cycloplegic refraction in children often reveals 1 to 2 diopters of hyperopia, which is the normal refractive error in this age group. The child described has age-appropriate vision and normal levels of hyperopia. Observation is the preferred management. As a result, full-time glasses, half-strength correction, and contact lenses are not necessary.

pool.q: What term describes the refractive error -0.25 +0.25 x 90?
pool.rationale: In simple hyperopic astigmatism, one focal line falls on the retina while the other focal line lies posterior to the retina. Similarly, in simple myopic astigmatism, one focal line falls on the retina, but the other focal line lies anterior to the retina. In compound hyperopic astigmatism, both focal lines lie posterior to the retina. In compound myopic astigmatism, both focal lines lie anterior to the retina. The power cross in the figure demonstrates that one axis is plano, with a focal line on the retina, while the other focal line is myopic and therefore anterior to the retina.

pool.q: What bifocal type results in the least amount of image jump?
pool.rationale:
Prism is induced when looking through a lens at any point besides its optical center. Therefore, when the eye is looking down and encounters the top of a bifocal add, the image jumps, unless the optical center of that bifocal add is right at the top of the segment. Executive style segments have their optical centers right at the top of the segment; therefore, they induce no image jump.
The optical center of a flat top segment is typically 3 mm from the top of the segment, whereas the optical center of a round top segment is much lower. Therefore, flat top segments cause some image jump, but less than that caused by round top segments.
The transition zone is the name for the area of "progressive" change in lens power in a progressive addition lens (PAL). While PALs do not induce image jump, they are (by definition) not bifocals.

pool.q: The American National Standards Institute (ANSI) and the International Standards Organization (ISO) require intraocular lenses (IOLs) with a power less than +25 D to be within what range of the labeled IOL power?
pool.rationale: IOLs with a power less than +25 D must be within 0.40 D of the labeled power. For IOLs between +25 and 30 D, the power must be within 0.50 D. For IOLs with a power greater than +30 D, the actual power must be within 1.0 D of the labeled power.

pool.q: What does the modulation transfer function graph of a bifocal intraocular lens (IOL) look like?
pool.rationale: The modulation transfer function describes an IOL's performance over a range of distances. For a bifocal IOL, the graphical representation of the modulation transfer function will show 2 distinct peaks (1 for distance and 1 for near). Similarly, a trifocal IOL has a modulation transfer function with 3 peaks. The newer, extended-depth-of-focus IOLs have modulation transfer functions without precipitous drops between peaks, thus reflecting better performance at intermediate focal lengths.

pool.q: What intervention has been shown to improve vision-related quality of life in patients with hemianopia?
pool.rationale: Although all of the choices (computer-based vision restoration therapy, electrical brain stimulation, scanning training, and sector prisms) have been explored for the treatment of homonymous hemianopic defects, scanning training (which can be provided by occupational therapists) has been shown to improve vision-related quality of life.

pool.q: In the setting of a posterior staphyloma, what is the simplest method to reliably obtain the refractive axial length in preparation for cataract surgery?
pool.rationale:
Optical biometry measures the axial length at the point of fixation, which can be helpful in patients with posterior staphyloma. A/B scan can also be helpful, but is more difficult to perform. Keratometry measures the cornea, not the axial length.
It can be difficult to obtain a good retina spike with ultrasonography when the fovea is on the sloping wall of a staphyloma. It may only be possible to obtain a good spike when the sound beam is directed eccentric to the fovea at the bottom of the staphyloma. This would result in an apparently longer axial length.

pool.q: The radius of curvature of a convex passenger-side automobile rear-view mirror is typically about 1.0 m. Where does such a mirror form an image of an object 10.0 m behind the car?

options.a: 1.0 m in front of the mirror
options.b: 0.47 m in front of the mirror
options.c: 0.47 m behind the mirror (ie, on the same side of the mirror as the source object)
options.d: 10.0 m in front of the mirror (ie, on the opposite side of the mirror from the source object)

pool.rationale: The power of the mirror is P = –2/r = –2.0 D. Thus, the vergence equation reads –1/10.0 + (–2.0) = 1/v so v = 1/(–2.1) = –0.47 m; that is 0.47 m away from the mirror on the side opposite the source object. This will be an erect, virtual image, minified by a factor of 0.47/10.0 = 0.047. Such a small image is interpreted by the driver as an object farther away than the original source object—as the reminder printed on the mirror suggests: “OBJECTS IN MIRROR ARE CLOSER THAN THEY APPEAR.”

pool.q: What is the typical refractive status of a human neonate?

pool.q: The American Academy of Ophthalmology’s Preferred Practice Pattern regarding vision rehabilitation recommends referral to low vision consultation when acuity falls below what level?
pool.rationale: The American Academy of Ophthalmology’s Preferred Practice Pattern regarding vision rehabilitation recommends that patients with acuity less than 20/40, contrast sensitivity loss, peripheral field loss, or central field loss be referred for low vision evaluation.

pool.q: What type of astigmatism best describes the eye with the following prescription?: + 0.50  - 1.00 x 90
pool.rationale:
Compound hyperopic astigmatism describes when both focal lines lie posterior to the retina. Compound myopic astigmatism describes when both focal lines lie anterior to the retina. Mixed astigmatism describes when one focal line lies anterior to the retina and the other focal line lies posterior to the retina.

For this question, the prescription can be converted into plus-cylinder as - 0.50 + 1.00 x 180 and is a Jackson cross, with one focal line anterior to the retina and one focal line posterior to the retina. While the overall spherical equivalent of this prescription is Plano, this is not emmetropia as there is still astigmatism present.

pool.q: A patient has a refractive error of -3.00 + 2.00 x 180. Keratometry readings are 44.00 at 90 degrees and 44.00 at 180 degrees. What type of contact lens would provide the best optical correction for this patient?
pool.rationale:
Contact lenses are useful for correcting most types of refractive errors. Spherical soft contact lenses do not correct for astigmatism, because they conform to the corneal topography.  In contrast, rigid gas permeable contact lenses will maintain their anterior curvature and the tear thickness under them will fill the gap by capillary action, which creates a tear meniscus that neutralizes the cylinder of the anterior corneal surface. Astigmatic errors of the eye may originate from the anterior corneal surface (most of astigmatism in typical patients), the posterior corneal surface, or the lens of the eye.
Soft toric contact lenses create no refractive tear meniscus, and thus the refractive correction toricity in the contact lens can neutralize anterior or posterior corneal astigmatism, as well as lenticular astigmatism.
A bitoric gas permeable lens has back toricity that is usually fit to or near the curvature of the cornea to maintain lens orientation, and can also have an anterior surface toricity to correct for lenticular or posterior corneal astigmatism.
In this example, the posterior surface needs of a bitoric contact lens would be spherical, and thus if there is astigmatic correction on the posterior surface, a tear meniscus would be created that would disturb the refractive correction of the eye. The alternative in a gas permeable lens would be one that only had anterior toricity instead of a bitoric design. Therefore, a toric soft contact lens would be the best lens in this example.

pool.q: What device can most accurately measure amplitude of accommodation?

pool.q: What is the procedure for measuring the reading add on a bifocal spectacle, using a lensometer (lensmeter)?

options.b: The front vertex of the lens is measured with the temple of the spectacles pointing toward the examiner.
options.c: The back vertex of the lens is measured with the temple of the spectacles pointing toward the examiner.
options.d: The front vertex of the lens is measured with the temple of the spectacles pointing away from the examiner.

pool.rationale: When measuring the power of a lens using a lensometer (lensmeter), the lens is placed on the nose cone initially, with the rear of the glass on the cone (temples of the spectacles away from the examiner) to measure the distance portion of the lens. To measure the bifocal portion of the lens or glasses, they are then turned around so that the temple section is facing toward the examiner (now the front of the lens is on the cone). Thus, the portion of the lens that is on the cone is the front vertex. Therefore, the statement that the temples are toward the examiner and the front vertex of the lens is being measured is correct. pool.q: What is the term for the disorder wherein corresponding retinal images of an object differ significantly in size?
pool.rationale:
Aniseikonia results from unequal magnification of image size between one eye and the other, which results in image size differences. Aniseikonia can manifest with symptoms of headache, dizziness, disorientation, and asthenopia. Aniseikonia is most often optically induced and secondary to anisometropia, the condition in which the eyes have unequal refractive error (naturally or secondary to refractive surgery, pseudophakic intraocular lens [IOL] implantation, or aphakia). However, aniseikonia can more uncommonly be induced by differences in retinal projection (ie, retinal stretching or foreshortening). Spectacle correction can cause individuals with significant anisometropia to experience aniseikonia because of differences between the eyes in image magnification.
Anisotropy refers to the condition of a material that exhibits different properties along different axes, such as polarized light. Anisocoria is unequal pupil size.

pool.q: For a thin lens with a power of +4.00 D, in air, what is the location of the image formed by an object 1 m to the left of the lens?
pool.rationale:
To calculate this answer, use the vergence equation, U + P = V. By convention, distances to the left of the interface are given a negative (-) sign, and distances to the right a positive (+) sign.

U + P = V
U = 1 (refractive index of air) / -1 (distance of object from lens)
P = +4.00 (power of lens)
V = 1 (refractive index of air) / v (distance of image from lens)

-1/1 + (+4) = 1/v
-1 + 4 = 1/v
3 = 1/v
3v = 1
v = 1/3 m to the right of the lens = 33 cm to the right of the lens

options.b: 1.50 diopters of astigmatism, steep corneal meridian at 140 degrees
options.c: 0.50 diopters of astigmatism, steep corneal meridian at 140 degrees
options.d: 1.50 diopters of astigmatism, steep corneal meridian at 50 degrees

pool.q: What part of the conoid of Sturm is on the retina if only a spherical lens is used to give the clearest image?
pool.rationale: Unlike light that passes through a spherical lens and is focused to a single point, light that passes through a spherocylindrical lens is not focused to a single point. Instead, the light is focused in a 3-dimensional image resembling a cone, which is termed conoid of Sturm. The length of the conoid increases with increases in the difference between the foci of the spherocylindrical lens. The images at the ends of the conoid are lines, and the image at the center of the conoid is a circle. Images between the ends and center of the conoid are elliptical in shape. The circle of least confusion is the circular cross section of the conoid of Sturm that is halfway between the 2 focal lines (the center of conoid is on the retina and shaped as a circle on the foveal photoreceptors); it provides the best visual acuity. During refraction, the clinician is manipulating the conoid of Sturm to maximize vision. This begins by placing the circle of least confusion on the retina by maximizing the sphere. Then the orientation of the conoid of Sturm is found by identifying the axis of astigmatism. Then the conoid of sturm is collapsed to a single point by negating the power of the astigmatism. Finally, the resultant point is placed on the retina by refining the sphere. The Jackson cross is not part of the conoid of Sturm.

pool.q: What optical advantage of a Galilean telescope is used by surgical loupes?

options.a: the positive objective lens, which makes the telescope compact
options.b: the distance between the lenses, which are separated by the sum of their focal lengths
options.c: all light is captured, making faint objects visible.
options.d: the image orientation, which is upright

pool.rationale: A focal systems are used clinically as telescopes or low vision aids. Surgical loupes are an example of a Galilean telescope, which has a high-powered negative ocular lens (eyepiece) and a low-powered positive objective lens; the lenses are separated by the difference between their focal lengths. The result is a compact telescope with an upright image. Galilean telescopes reflect some light, whereas Keplerian telescopes (ie, astronomical telescopes, which have 2 positive lenses separated by the sum of their focal lengths, which makes them longer) capture all light, and are ideal for visualizing faint objects.

pool.q: How much does a 15D prism bend light, in degrees?
pool.rationale: A useful rule of thumb is that for small angles, a prism diopter produces a little more than half a degree of deviation. Thus, a 15Δ prism produces slightly more than 7.5° of deviation, so the only reasonable choice is 8.53°. Alternatively, the exact value can be calculated. A 15Δ prism deflects light 15 cm at a distance of 100 cm. The tangent of the angle of the deflection is 15/100; the angle, therefore, is arctan (0.15) = 8.53°.

pool.q: What is the spherical equivalent of +1.00 - 2.00 x 90?

In other words, the spherical equivalent is the dioptric midpoint of a spherocylindrical lens where the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the blurred image are approximately equal. The goal of refraction is to choose a lens that places the circle of least confusion on the retina. Spherical equivalent is calculated by adding the sphere and half of the cylinder. In this case, +1.00 sphere added to ½*(-2.00) is 0.

pool.q: What happens from birth to age 6 years to keep the eyes emmetropic?

However, most children's eyes are actually emmetropic, with only a 2% incidence of myopia at 6 years. This phenomenon is due to a still-undetermined mechanism called emmetropization. During this period of eye growth, a compensatory loss of 4 D of corneal power and 2D of lens power keeps most eyes close to emmetropia.

pool.q: In this scenario, a distant object is located to the left of a lens system, which focuses light from this object at +1.0 m to the right of the lens system. If a +3.00 lens is added immediately adjacent to the lens system, where is the new image located?

options.b: 25 cm to the right of the lenses
options.c: 50 cm to the right of the lenses

pool.q: According to studies, what therapy is best suited to have a protective effect against the progression of myopia in childhood?
pool.rationale:
Because accommodation is a postulated mechanism for the progression of myopia, optical correction through the use of bifocal or multifocal spectacles or the removal of distance spectacles when performing close work has been recommended to reduce the progression of myopia. Administration of atropine eyedrops also has long been proposed because it inhibits accommodation, which may exert forces on the eye that result in axial elongation. Studies have suggested a protective effect of low-dose atropine (eg, 0.01% eye drops), even in the absence of evident cycloplegia. Use of a drug that lowers intraocular pressure has been suggested as an alternative pharmacologic intervention; this approach works presumably by reducing internal pressure on the eyewall. It has also been postulated that use of rigid contact lenses could slow the progression of myopia in children. Visual training purported to reduce myopia includes convergence exercises and those that incorporate changes in near–far focus.
High concentrations of 10% or 1% atropine are not required nor more effective than 0.01% atropine. Studies demonstrate that outdoor activities may have some protective effect, not indoor activities.

pool.q: What factor increases the likelihood of decentration of the laser ablation in noncustom laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) or photorefractive keratectomy (PRK)?
pool.rationale:
The angle kappa (κ) is the angle between the visual axis and the pupillary axis. When there is a large difference between these 2 lines (angle κ is large), there is a higher potential for decentration. Custom surgery, where there is correction for the visual axis and the pupillary position, can reduce this problem.
Large pupil size may be associated with postrefractive surgery glare, haloes, and other night vision issues, not with decentered ablations. Risk of decentration is increased with hyperopic, not myopic ablations. Corneal thickness has minimal effect on decentration.

options.c: Refine the final sphere with a trial frame in a longer hallway (6 meters).
options.d: Take no additional step. The refraction should be correct as measured.

pool.rationale: Refracting in a short room is inherently inaccurate because normal fogging techniques to relax accommodation will not be effective. Another option would be to install mirrors to optically extend the room length to 6 meters.

pool.q: What slit-lamp biomicroscopy technique is best for viewing the corneal endothelial cell pattern?
pool.rationale:
With an ordinary slit lamp, the outlines of individual endothelial cells are best seen by viewing the specular reflection of a narrow slit beam at high magnification. A wider field can be viewed using a specular microscope, with a contact optical system to decrease surface reflections.
The slit-lamp is designed to provide a variety of illumination techniques allowing for examination of the anterior segment in a variety of ways.
  • Direct focal illumination. This is the most commonly used examination technique, in which the examiner focuses on the area directly illuminated by the slit.
  • Retroillumination. The beam can be decentered, so that it is striking the iris, with the examiner focusing with the microscope in front, on the cornea, for example. This enables the observer to see corneal opacities illuminated against the black pupil by the reflected light from the iris (iris retroillumination). As another example, by shining the beam through the edge of the pupil, one can observe opacities in the cornea, iris, and lens retroilluminated by the reflected light from the fundus.
  • Sclerotic scatter. The slit beam is decentered so that it strikes the junction between sclera and cornea, causing light to be totally internally reflected, like a fiber-optic light pipe. In this manner, light follows its longest possible path through the cornea and makes nebular opacities more visible against a dark pupil background.
  • Specular reflection. By looking directly at the bright reflection of the slit beam under high magnification, the examiner can observe irregularities in the corneal surface and see the endothelial cell pattern (this is the principle underlying specular microscopy).

pool.q: For a patient with mild corneal edema and the findings shown in the image below, what history would support the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Many different conditions can lead to corneal edema, including trauma, infection, hypoxia, toxicity of topical or intraocular pharmacologic agents, and endothelial dystrophies. The slit-lamp image above shows a peripheral pannus, which can be found in patients with contact lens overwear. Hypoxia from contact lens overwear can result in typically mild corneal edema along with corneal pannus.
Although a palmar rash can suggest syphilis, which can lead to interstitial keratitis, the photo does not depict this. Similarly, corneal pannus is not usually seen with glaucoma or recent cataract surgery, even though edema can be found in these cases.

pool.q: The Abbe number is a measure of what characteristic of a lens?

options.c: thickness required to achieve an optical power

pool.rationale:
The Abbe number is a measure of chromatic aberration. The lower the Abbe number, the higher the amount of chromatic aberration present in the lens material. Spectacle lenses with a low Abbe number often require antireflective coating to minimize chromatic aberration that arises, particularly when bright indoor light reflects off the lenses.
Lens materials made from materials with higher refractive index require less thickness than a lens material with lower refractive index to achieve the same optical power.
Polycarbonate for instance is a high refractive index and highly impact-resistant material. This allows for a light, thin, durable lens. A disadvantage of polycarbonate is the high degree of chromatic aberration (low Abbe number). Standard lens material (CR-39) and polycarbonate both absorb most UV light.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is selecting an intraocular lens (IOL) for an upcoming unilateral pediatric cataract surgery on an 18-month-old child who refracts to +2.00 sphere in the fellow eye. What is the most important consideration when choosing the IOL and power?

options.a: lack of accommodation from the monofocal IOL
options.b: myopic shift as the patient reaches adulthood
options.c: the refractive error of the fellow eye
options.d: the myopia of the patient's older sibling

pool.rationale:
When selecting an IOL for pediatric eyes, the most important consideration is the myopic shift that the eye will undergo as the patient reaches adulthood. There are many ways to deal with this. One could implant 2 or more IOLs simultaneously in a piggyback configuration, with the patient's expected adult emmetropic power most posterior. As the child matures, the anterior IOL or IOLs will be removed with further surgeries. Another option would be to implant an IOL for emmetropia now and plan for future corneal refractive surgery to address the subsequent myopia. A third option would be to implant an IOL with the adult emmetropic power and use contact lenses to address the childhood hyperopia.
Children with accommodation in one eye function well and the use of multifocal IOLs in pediatric patients is controversial. The patient's current refraction in the fellow eye is normal and IOL choice should be based on biometry and the plan for the myopic shift. The refractive status of an older sibling should have minimal impact on the IOL choice.

pool.q: A 68-year-old man developed a corneal ulcer and was left with a visually significant central corneal scar after the ulcer was adequately treated. A penetrating keratoplasty (PK) is recommended to improve his vision. Additionally, he has a 3+ nuclear sclerotic cataract in the same eye. What is the recommended approach to calculating intraocular lens (IOL) power in this case?

options.a: Calculate IOL power based on optical biometry measurements in the fellow (unaffected) eye prior to a combined PK + cataract extraction / implantation of IOL procedure.
options.b: Calculate IOL power based on optical biometry measurements in the affected eye prior to a combined PK + cataract extraction / implantation of IOL procedure.
options.c: Calculate IOL power based on optical biometry measurements in the affected eye prior to a cataract extraction / implantation of IOL procedure, then complete the PK several months later, when the corneal wounds have healed completely.
options.d: Calculate IOL power based on optical biometry measurements in the affected eye after complete healing of the PK.

pool.rationale:
It is difficult to predict ultimate corneal power after a penetrating keratoplasty (PK). Therefore, the recommended approach, when both PK and cataract extraction are needed, is to complete the PK and allow for complete healing of the graft prior to calculation of IOL power, with a second surgery for cataract extraction and implantation of the IOL.
If simultaneous PK and IOL implantation are necessary, then IOL calculations based on the fellow eye may be an option, but there likely will be error with this approach. The other options (calculation based on optical biometry measurements in the affected eye prior to a combined PK + cataract extraction / implantation of IOL procedure, or calculation based on optical biometry measurements in the affected eye prior to a cataract extraction / implantation of IOL procedure, then complete the PK several months later, when the corneal wounds have healed completely) are not likely to produce satisfactory results.

pool.q: A 78-year-old patient has cataract surgery in the right eye. Postoperatively, the patient complains of headache and dizziness. The postoperative refractive error is -0.75 sph with vision of 20/25. The left eye has a refractive error of +2.25+1.50×27, a 2+ nuclear sclerotic cataract, and vision of 20/60. pool.q: What characteristic of the interaction between light and tissue is used by the scanning laser polarimeter to measure thickness of the nerve fiber layer?
pool.rationale:
The retinal nerve fiber layer is birefringent, meaning it polarizes light or changes the polarization of incident light that passes through it. The scanning laser polarimeter uses this property to measure nerve fiber layer thickness. The cornea is also birefringent, so a corneal compensator is necessary to eliminate the cornea’s polarization effects.
Interferometry is the basic principle upon which optical coherence tomography works.
Fluorescence angiography and autofluorescence are made possible by the shift in frequency in photons absorbed by and emitted by tissue (Stokes shift).
Diffraction is the tendency of light to spread out as it passes through an aperture. There are numerous applications in ophthalmology. Among other things, diffraction sets a limit on the resolution that can be achieved in any optical instrument (including the eye).

pool.q: Following penetrating keratoplasty, a patient has cataract surgery with the postoperative topography shown. What management is recommended for this patient?

Gas-permeable or other rigid contact lenses neutralize irregular astigmatism because tear fluid fills the irregular space between the lens and cornea. LASIK and limbal relaxing incisions would be contraindicated in this case, as they unpredictably deal with irregular astigmatism. Long-term corticosteroid treatment is indicated for penetrating keratoplasty, but it would not treat irregular astigmatism.

pool.q: When examining an eye with small pupils using a head-mounted, binocular, indirect ophthalmoscope, what adjustment can improve binocular visualization?

options.a: reducing the distance between the observer's head and the patient
options.b: narrowing the observer's effective interpupillary distance
options.c: moving the ophthalmoscope's mirror away from the observer

pool.rationale: When looking through a small pupil, the observer can improve visualization by narrowing their effective interpupillary distance. This can be accomplished by several means. Moving the ophthalmoscope's mirror closer to the observer (the small-pupil feature available on some ophthalmoscopes) decreases the distance between the light paths to the observer's left and right eyes, effectively narrowing the observer's interpupillary distance. If the examiner can slightly converge, it will narrow the observer's effective interpupillary distance. Increasing the distance between the observer and the patient decreases the angle formed by the observer's 2 eyes and the patient's eye, thereby allowing the light paths from the observer's eyes to "squeeze through" a smaller pupil.

pool.q: What methods can be employed to reduce the risk of night vision difficulties such as glare, starbursts, and haloes in patients who will undergo keratorefractive surgery?

options.b: decreasing the size of optical zone
options.c: creation of a transition zone 0.5 mm to 1.0 mm larger than the pupil

pool.rationale:
Postoperative night-vision problems are well-described and are often associated with large pupil sizes (≥ 8 mm). These symptoms, which include the appearance of glare, starbursts, and haloes, decreased contrast sensitivity, and decreased quality of vision at night, tend to occur in patients with both large pupils and small treatment zones (≤ 6 mm).
In appropriate candidates, third-generation lasers utilize larger optical and transition zones to help reduce the incidence and severity of night-vision problems. The accepted standard transition zone between ablated and unablated cornea is 0.5 mm-1.0 mm larger than the pupil to help reduce night-vision problems, but in order to conserve corneal tissue, smaller optical zones are used in the correction of high myopia. pool.q: What characterizes the interaction of the excimer laser with ocular tissues?
pool.rationale:
The excimer laser (an excited dimer of argon and fluorine) has sufficient energy to rupture carbon-carbon and carbon-nitrogen bonds, a process called photoablation. Photoablation ruptures the collagen polymer into small fragments and expels a small depth of corneal tissue with each pulse. However, it has very low tissue penetration. Because of this, it does not damage adjacent tissue significantly, or accelerate the growth of cataracts. Most of its energy is focused on the cornea, with very little thermal spread in the surrounding tissue.
Photodisruption describes the laser-tissue interaction converting tissue to plasma from the high energy of the laser, leading to formation of cavitations or shockwaves that are used to break down tissues. Examples include Nd:YAG lasers and femtosecond lasers.
Photochemical activation, or photoactivation, uses the interaction of a long exposure time laser with a photosensitizing dye (eg, verteporfin) acting as a chemical catalyst to create a photochemical reaction only in tissues where the dye is present.
Photocoagulation occurs when tissue absorbs light and converts it to heat, causing denaturation. Examples of photocoagulation lasers are argon and diode lasers.

pool.q: Why might bifocal spectacles slow the progression of myopia?

pool.q: Corneal haze secondary to corneal edema is primarily caused by what light phenomenon?
pool.rationale:
Light scattering occurs when small particles suspended in a transparent medium interfere with the transmittance of light and cause photons to deviate from a straight path. Short wavelengths of light are scattered more strongly than are longer wavelengths. Larger particles scatter light more intensely than do smaller particles. In a healthy cornea, the tightly arranged and regularly spaced collagen molecules minimize the effects of scattering. When a cornea becomes edematous, excess fluid in the stroma disrupts the regular collagen structure, causing light scattering.
Diffraction may be thought of as light, when encountering an obstacle, scattering off in different directions at the edges. What really happens is that light interacts with the electrons in the material, most noticeably with the electrons at the edges. Once light scatters off in different directions, it usually interferes with other parts of the diffracted light. Hence, in classical wave theory, the phenomenon of diffraction of light, as it passes beyond an obstacle of comparable size to its wavelength, is generally described as interference effects of the emerging light.

pool.q: A patient with a 10-year history of contact lens wear is found to have bilateral superficial corneal neovascularization extending 1 mm beyond the superior limbus. What is the best first step in treatment?

options.b: switch to a contact lens with increased oxygen permeability
options.c: argon laser photocoagulation to ablate large vessels

Neovascularization is a common condition in chronic contact lens wearers, especially with overuse. The lenses cause chronic hypoxia that induces blood vessel growth. Patients can have superficial, deep, sectoral, or 360 degrees of neovascularization. If patients have significant vascularization, stopping contact lens wear may be the best treatment. Contact lenses can also cause superficial punctate keratitis (especially 3 o'clock and 9 o’clock staining), giant papillary conjunctivitis, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis, corneal edema, corneal infiltrates (hypoxic, infectious), and corneal warpage. Trachoma is a bilateral keratoconjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. pool.q: What type of intraocular lens (IOL) uses concentric refractive rings of different optical powers?

The posterior surface has a stepped structure, and the diffraction from these multiple rings produces a second image, with an effective add power.

pool.q: A subjective refraction is being performed on a young myopic patient. After determining the sphere and cylinder correction, the ophthalmologist performs the duochrome test to verify the spherical endpoint. The ophthalmologist slightly fogs the eye by adding 0.5D of sphere in the phoropter. What is the next step in the procedure?

options.a: Verify that the patient sees the green side as sharper and add minus power until both the red and green sides are equally sharp.
options.b: Verify that the patient sees the red side as sharper and add minus power until both the red and green sides are equally sharp.
options.c: Verify that the patient sees the red side as sharper and add plus power until both the red and green sides are equally sharp.
options.d: Verify that the patient sees the green side as sharper and add plus power until both the red and green sides are equally sharp.

The duochrome test uses chromatic aberration to verify the spherical endpoint of a refraction. The letters on the green side, with shorter wavelength, are focused in front of the letters on the red side with the longer wavelength. The eye should optimally focus between the red and green wavelengths, making the letters on each side equally sharp.
Start the test by adding plus power to slightly fog the eye until the letters on the red side appear sharper. Minus power is then added until letters on both sides are equally sharp. In a young patient, starting with the green side sharper can lead to overminusing the patient. The mnemonic "RAM-GAP" can be used to remember how to perform the test: Red add minus; green add plus.

pool.q: What is the primary reason that patients with presbyopia cannot tolerate a large amount of anisometropia in bifocal lenses?

With a bifocal segment, the gaze is usually directed 8–10 mm below and 1.5–3.0 mm nasal to the distance optical center of the distance lens (in the following examples, we assume the usual 8 mm down and 2 mm nasal). As long as the bifocal segments are of the same power and type, the induced, vertical prismatic displacement is determined by the powers of the distance lens alone. If the lens powers are the same for the 2 eyes, the displacement of each is the same. However, if the patient’s vision is anisometropic, a phoria is induced by the unequal prismatic displacement of the 2 lenses. The amount of vertical phoria is determined by subtracting the smaller prismatic displacement from the larger if both lenses are myopic or hyperopic or by adding the 2 lenses if the patient is hyperopic in 1 eye and myopic in the other.
Image jump refers to the change in the position of objects viewed as one comes to the line of a bifocal segment. It can be minimized by moving the optical center of the add closer to the top of the segment as in a flat-top or executive style bifocal.
Aniseikonia is defined as a difference in image size between the 2 eyes and can cause disturbances in stereopsis. Generally, a person can tolerate spherical aniseikonia of 5%–8%. In clinical practice, aniseikonia is rarely a significant problem; however, it should be considered in patients with unexplained vision symptoms.

pool.q: What is the cause of presbyopia according to the theory of von Helmholtz?

pool.q: Where is the intermediate image formed by the first lens?

options.a: 0.5 m to the right of the lens
options.b: 2.0 m to the left of the lens
options.c: 2.0 m to the right of the lens
options.d: 0.5 m to the left of the lens

pool.rationale: Vergence is the ratio of refractive index, n, divided by the distance from the object or to the image. Vergence (in diopters) = n/distance (in meters). The first lens adds an additional –1.00 D of vergence. Light leaving the lens therefore has a vergence of –2.00 D. pool.q: What property of light results in the white appearance of sclera?

There may be various visual effects, depending on the size of the particle and the wavelength of incident light. Rayleigh scattering occurs with very small particles (up to 1/10 of the wavelength of the incident light); iris color occurs as a result of Rayleigh scattering. Mie scattering occurs with slightly larger particles (1 or more wavelengths larger than the incident light); sclera and clouds appear white as a result of Mie scattering. The Tyndall effect occurs with large particles, such as cells within the aqueous humor. Light absorption, reflection, and transmission are principles of the electromagnetic wave theory of light and describe the effects of light through uniform media, such as air or glass.

pool.q: What is the mechanism through which the femtosecond laser interacts with tissues?

Contiguous photodisruption allows for creation of the corneal flap, channel, or incision. Photothermal laser effects cause tissue modification as illustrated by use of a holmium:YAG laser. Heat is generated that results in collagen shrinkage. An example of photoablation is the excimer laser used in LASIK and photorefractive keratectomy. This process breaks chemical bonds within tissue. Photocoagulation is primarily used in retina lasers and results in a thermal burn to tissue.

pool.q: What therapy or intervention has been associated with peripheral corneal neovascularization, microcystic epitheliopathy, and immune hypersensitivity reactions?
